transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-07
Time: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~52m
Attendees: Priya (Redwood AE), Evan (Redwood SE), Maya (Redwood SRE), Carlos (Finova Lead ML Eng), Aisha (Finova Infra), Tom (Finova CTO)

Summary: quick stability deep-dive. Customer seeing intermittent OOMs & CUDA errors when running long-context scoring/serving workload. We walked through batching, KV cache patterns, quantization impacts, and retry semantics. Next: share logs, config, and benchmark spreadsheet; SE to propose mitigations.

Topics: OOM patterns, CUDA driver/oom traces, timeout/retry semantics, batching & prefix cache interactions, quantization tradeoffs, VPC/on-prem nuances.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Priya (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll run about 45-60 minutes, quick intros then Evan will drive the technical portion.
[00:18] Carlos (Finova): thanks, yes we appreciate it, been blocked by random OOMs and a few timeouts in our prod-like POC.
[00:25] Evan (Redwood SE): cool, can you give a short repro surface? e.g., sequence lengths, batch sizes, quantization, GPU types?
[00:37] Carlos: sure. most requests are conversational scoring where we append a long history, 1-3 inputs pe tokenized, max-seq we've seen is ~6k tokens, average 1.2k. batch sizes vary 1-8 depending on traffic. we're on A100s in their cloud (weirdly one cluster is older driver). we tried int8 quant and saw slightly more stability? uh, wait — less stable actually, we saw more OOM spikes after quantization.
[00:58] Aisha (Infra): also a couple of calls show CUDA launch failures and then a bunch of timeouts from our sidecar proxy.
[01:10] Evan: got it. common pattern: long context + kv cache + batching = high peak memory from KV + activation spikes during generation. quantization reduces model weight memory but can change kernel choices that increase activation memory or change workspace needs.
[01:28] Maya (Redwood SRE): and drivers/backwards-compat cuDNN versions can flip which kernels are picked. sometimes the int8 path triggers a different fused kernel with larger temp workspace. we've seen this with older drivers.
[01:45] Tom (CTO): so the quant made it worse? that seems counterintuitive.
[01:50] Evan: yeah so quick note: weight quant reduces model param memory but can increase per-step workspace or lead to less optimal matmul kernels. if your runtime picks a different kernel it may require more scratch memory. plus mixed precision/caching interplay can be surprising.
[02:05] Carlos: here's a snippet from our 03:12 crash, it shows "CUDA out of memory" then a "cuBLAS kernel launch failed". sometimes the process kills itself, sometimes just timeouts upstream.
[02:20] Priya: we'll take those logs; Evan will map them to typical causes and checklist items.
[02:26] Evan: first checklist: 1) confirm driver/cuDNN/CUDA versions across nodes, 2) max-seqlen distribution, 3) per-request batch vs micro-batch behavior, 4) whether KV cache is fully materialized for all shards, 5) whether we're using persistent KV vs ephemeral.
[02:45] Carlos: noted. our max-seq distribution is heavy-tail; ~5% of requests end up >3.5k tokens. we didn't limit input length at gateway because business wanted full history.
[02:55] Evan: that explains spikes. If you have unbounded tails the rare large request will blow up peak memory. recommended mitigations are prefix truncation, partial KV offload, or throttling/early rejection of super-long requests at the edge.
[03:12] Speaker 1: (mumbling) also batching policy matters — a big batch with one long example can blow up memory for all items in the batch.
[03:23] Aisha: we use dynamic batching in the sidecar, up to 8.
[03:28] Evan: consider dynamic batch limits that are length-aware. Redwood has batch shapers that can split or isolate long-context requests. we'll share config examples.
[03:40] Carlos: what about retry semantics? our infra retries on transient timeouts, which means we end up with duplicate heavy requests and further pressure.
[03:48] Maya: right — retries can amplify the spike. recommended: idempotent request tokens + client-side backoff + server-side early-rate-limit on resource-intense requests.
[03:57] Evan: for retries we also suggest different error classes: "retryable small" vs "retryable heavy". heavy requests should return a 429-like signal so client doesn't immediately retry. and Redwood can be configured to return a 503 with Retry-After when the scheduler is overloaded.
[04:14] Tom: we're on a VPC/private deployment; any differences vs hosted?
[04:20] Evan: on private you control drivers and GPUs; so you'll need to ensure driver homogeneity and tested cuDNN combos. hosted pulleys we manage the stack and can roll optimizations faster, but private gives you control. tradeoff: on-prem means you must coordinate kernel/driver updates.
[04:36] Carlos: we did notice one node had NVIDIA driver 520 and others 530. could that cause the kernel selection mismatch?
[04:44] Evan: absolutely. different minor driver versions or cuDNN can pick very different kernels. that can explain intermittent OOM on just some shards.
[04:54] Priya: can you also share the GPU instance types? we want to map memory & scratch profiles.
[04:58] Carlos: mainly A100 40GB and a few older A100 80GB — oh wait that was a mistake, it's 80GB and 40GB mixed.
[05:07] Evan: mixing 40GB and 80GB will result in scheduler complexity — Redwood will try to allocate but you may see OOMs when the request hits a 40GB node. pinning pools or labeling is best.
[05:16] Aisha: noted. we can label nodes by mem size.
[05:19] Carlos: what about KV cache memory? are we duplicating KV across replicas?
[05:24] Evan: depends on config. some modes replicate KV per replica for lowest latency; others shard. replication means more memory used overall but simpler assembly. sharding reduces per-node memory but increases network cost and complexity. if you replicate KV and mix large and small GPUs you may run into OOM on small GPUs.
[05:41] Carlos: our current config replicates KV, to minimize cross-node fetches.
[05:46] Evan: that would explain. two paths: move to shard-KV for very long histories, or enforce length-based routing (route long requests to 80GB pool).
[05:56] Tom: is there an automated fallback where we do an approximate (shorter) scoring when we detect imminent OOM?
[06:03] Maya: we have graceful degradation features — you can configure an automatic fallback to a smaller model variant or a truncated prefix path. it's not magic; you need to define policies and acceptable quality loss.
[06:16] Carlos: hmmm we'd prefer not to reduce accuracy silently; need to log and surface to app.
[06:21] Priya: agreed, Redwood can surface a reason code in the response when fallback occurs so your app can decide to show a degraded but safe response.
[06:30] Evan: another root cause: workspace fragmentation in long-lived processes. If your process handles many different sequence lengths over time the allocator can fragment; restart cadence or memory compaction can help. we recommend monitoring native allocator metrics.
[06:46] Carlos: we run the runtime in single long-lived container per node. restarting more often is painful. any other levers?
[06:53] Evan: try enabling memory pooling with large block alloc and reuse; or use the persistent-kv mode which can reuse allocations. also set aggressive batch timeouts so a single long request doesn't hold batch slots too long.
[07:09] Aisha: about timeouts — our sidecar defaults to 60s, but some gen workloads take longer and then the proxy kills it and retries. should we increase sidecar timeout?
[07:18] Evan: longer timeouts help for slow but healthy generation, but they can also lead to resource tying. best is to have per-route SLOs and tell the client via Retry-After or early signals. Also consider streaming so the client gets partial results earlier.
[07:31] Carlos: we already stream but heavy scoring calls still block.
[07:35] Evan: also check tokenization mismatches: if client and server tokenize differently you can hit higher-than-expected token counts.
[07:44] Carlos: good call, we'll validate tokenizers.
[07:47] Speaker 2: (brief crosstalk)
[07:50] Evan: quick bit on CUDA errors: if you see launch failures followed by OOM, it sometimes indicates a failed kernel allocation that falls back to a different kernel that uses more memory; the trace in the runtime logs + cuda-memcheck can reveal this. attach stack trace and we can map.
[08:06] Carlos: we ran cuda-memcheck once but it was noisy. we'll re-run with a smaller reproducer.
[08:12] Evan: please capture the runtime memory map (pmap equivalent) at failure time — that helps.
[08:18] Priya: are there recommended cuDNN versions for int8 paths?
[08:22] Evan: we maintain a matrix; generally newer cuDNN 9.x with specific minor versions is best, but it's model and kernel dependent. I'll share the matrix and the specific kernels we've seen problematic.
[08:34] Tom: any quick config knobs we can flip to mitigate today?
[08:37] Evan: yes: 1) enforce max-seqlen 4096 at edge or route >4096 to a dedicated 80GB pool, 2) disable aggressive batching for large inputs (set batch cap by tokens not just count), 3) for int8 try fallback to mixed precision or a different quantizer, 4) enable early reject/429 for heavy requests when queue depth high, 5) align driver/cuDNN across nodes.
[09:00] Carlos: for (3) how do we test quantizer impact without risking prod?
[09:05] Evan: run offline benchmarks on a dev pool with identical drivers, try int8 vs int4 vs fp16 and record both memory and latency profiles. Redwood has a benchmark harness we'll share that automates sweeping quant and batch configs.
[09:18] Priya: we'll attach that harness + sample deck.
[09:22] Aisha: about observability — we need token-level memory and per-request allocation traces. do you expose that?
[09:29] Maya: we emit allocation metrics and per-request peak memory tags in the runtime; you can ingest into Prometheus/Datadog. we'll also add a flag to dump per-request alloc snapshots when a fatal OOM occurs.
[09:41] Carlos: perfect, that would speed root cause analysis.
[09:45] Evan: last technical note: caching strategy. If you pre-warm KV for a long conversation you can reduce per-request peak, but pre-warming itself allocates memory. tradeoffs. for bursts, a sharded KV approach with on-demand fetch is usually best.
[09:59] Carlos: any recommended retry backoff parameters? our current is immediate x3.
[10:04] Evan: immediate retries are bad for heavy requests. use exponential backoff w/ jitter starting at 200-500ms for short ops, but for heavy ops consider a longer initial backoff (1-2s) and a max 10s, or better use queue tokens so clients can poll for completion.
[10:20] Priya: wrapping up—I'll enumerate hi-priority action items and share the POC benchmark. Evan will produce a mitigation guide.
[10:28] Tom: timeline: we need stable POC in 2 weeks to present to ops. is that feasible?
[10:34] Evan: yes if we get logs + traces quickly and apply short-term knobs (route long to 80GB, length-aware batching, tweak quantization) we can stabilize.
[10:42] Carlos: we'll get those artifacts to you by Friday.
[10:46] Priya: great. any other questions?
[10:50] Carlos: none from me. thanks all.
[10:52] Priya: thanks everyone, follow up email with links, configs, and the benchmark harness.

End transcript.
